title: Scheduling: Taints, Tolerations & Draining Nodes
intro: Sometimes a pod won't schedule, or you need to safely take a node out of rotation for maintenance. This is how you control where pods do and don't run.

steps.prompt: List the nodes in the cluster with extra detail.
steps.fake_output:
NAME     STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
node-1   Ready    <none>  30d   v1.29.0
node-2   Ready    <none>  30d   v1.29.0
steps.explanation: -o wide adds extra columns like internal IP and OS image — the plain 'get nodes' only shows status and age.
steps.why: 'kubectl describe node <name>' gives you way more (capacity, allocated resources, taints) for one node at a time — 'get nodes -o wide' is for scanning all of them quickly.

steps.prompt: Mark node-2 as unschedulable so no new pods land there (you're about to do maintenance).
steps.explanation: Cordon only blocks NEW pods — existing pods on node-2 keep running untouched.
steps.why: This is deliberately less disruptive than drain — cordon is the first step when you want to stop new scheduling without yet evicting anything.

steps.prompt: Now actually evict the existing pods off node-2 safely, ignoring DaemonSet-managed pods.
steps.fake_output:
node/node-2 already cordoned
evicting pod default/web-abc
node/node-2 drained
steps.explanation: Drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets and gracefully evicts pods (letting Deployments reschedule them elsewhere) rather than just killing them.
steps.why: --ignore-daemonsets is required because DaemonSet pods are meant to run on every node and would otherwise block the drain forever, since they can't be 'moved' anywhere else.

steps.prompt: Maintenance done — bring node-2 back into rotation.
steps.explanation: This just undoes the cordon — new pods can schedule there again. It does NOT move the pods that got drained away back.
steps.why: There's no 'undrain' — uncordon only reopens scheduling; anything that moved off during drain stays where it rescheduled to.
